summary: The note describes how the community of Harrison Meadows is tackling the digital divide in education, tracing it from the 1990s introduction of computer-based learning to today's issues of connectivity and digital literacy. It covers initiatives such as the Tech for All program, Connect Harrison, Laptops for Learning, library workshops, and supporting legislation. Personal stories from students, adult learners and educators illustrate the impact, while noting that challenges remain.
one_line: Harrison Meadows combats the educational digital divide through school programs, library workshops, donations, policy changes and community coalitions.
key_facts: The Harrison Meadows initiative to address the digital divide in education was described as commencing on November 7, 2023.

Retired teacher Jenna Patterson recalls that around September 1995 local schools began using computer-based learning, but they had only one computer lab that was hard to access, and educators lacked training.

At an October 12, 2023 town hall meeting, Educational Consultant Michael Torres said the divide is no longer just physical equipment but the understanding and skills to navigate the digital landscape.
The 'homework gap', a term that gained traction in the late 2010s, refers to difficulty completing assignments requiring online resources for students without home internet access.
On January 15, 2024, the Harrison Meadows School District launched the 'Tech for All' program, aiming to provide every student with a laptop and home internet access.
Local libraries offered free courses and IT support; library director Samuel Johnson said, 'We want technology to be a bridge, not a barrier.'
Legislation passed on September 3, 2023 offered financial incentives for internet service providers to improve connectivity in underserved areas.
The 'Connect Harrison' coalition was established on February 11, 2024 to identify and resolve connectivity issues for students.
The 'Laptops for Learning' campaign launched on March 17, 2024, with local businesses donating pre-owned computers to be refurbished and given to students in need.
The local high school held its first 'Digital Day' on May 25, 2024, covering digital tools, coding basics and online safety.
Fifteen-year-old Maria Gonzales, whose only prior internet access was a shared family phone with limited data, now uses upgraded school Wi-Fi and a Tech for All laptop to pursue graphic design.
Victor Lee, 42, returned to school and credits the digital literacy workshops with helping him get 'ahead of the curve'.
School Board President Angela Davis called the digital divide 'a systemic issue that affects every aspect of teaching and learning'.
